attributes.body:
や is a particle that has several different roles in Japanese, with the most common being as an adverbial particle. や is used similarly to と as 'and', but rather than listing specific things in a group, it lists 'things like (A)'.

や is always used to group nouns, and simply comes directly after them.

To compare how と and や are different, imagine that there is a bowl of fruit. In this bowl there are apples, oranges, and peaches. If と is used to list the apples and oranges, it would give the listener the impression that there are no peaches. This is called an 'exhaustive' list, meaning that all possibilities should be listed. However, if や is used, the listener would know that there are other things in the bowl apart from the apples and oranges. In this way, や is a better choice when you want to say 'and', but don't want to limit the group that you are listing.

Caution

や cannot be used after verb phrases. This is done with たり, or とか.

attributes.source: [DBJG] A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

attributes.description: Japanese Particles と (to), や (ya), か (ka)

attributes.body: ら is a pluralizing suffix that attaches to nouns to mean '(A) and others'. や is a particle that links multiple nouns, similar to 'and' in English. While ら can follow a single noun, や must connect two or more. Both imply the presence of other people or things not explicitly mentioned.

と and や are particles used to connect nouns, similar to 'and' in English, but differ slightly. と is used when listing all items explicitly (e.g., りんごとバナナ = 'apples and bananas [only]'). In contrast, や indicates examples from a larger set (e.g., りんごやバナナ = 'things like apples and bananas,' implying there are others).

Both および and や are used to list items, but they differ in nuance and formality. および is a highly formal expression similar to と, often implying a complete list. It is used almost exclusively in writing and structured, formal speech. In contrast, や is less formal and suggests a partial list, such as 'A, B, and things like that.'

Both や and やら～やら are used to list items or examples from a larger set, and are more common in writing or formal speech than in casual conversation. や is a straightforward way to suggest other similar examples, as in 'A, B, and things like that.' In contrast, やら～やら carries a stronger nuance of uncertainty or possibility, as if the speaker is listing examples that may or may not apply.

second_relatable.title: やら～やら
second_relatable.meaning: Whether or, Things like, And … so on

attributes.body: Both や and とか～とか are used to list items non-exhaustively, implying that other, unmentioned items are also included. や is more common in writing or formal speech, while とか is more colloquial. や must follow nouns, while とか can also be used with actions or events involving verbs. Additionally, とか can follow each item in the list, whereas や is not used after the final item.

second_relatable.title: とか～とか
second_relatable.meaning: Among other things, For example, Such as

attributes.body: Both たり～たりする and や can be used to provide or list examples, similar to the English 'things like A and B.' The main difference is that たり can only be used with verbs, adjectives, or noun phrases, while や can only be used to list nouns. Note that both grammar points suggest that the speaker is listing just some of many possible actions or things.
